summary: The Chronicle, a state-owned newspaper, reports President Irfaan Ali told relatives at the Charity Waterfront on Wednesday 22 July that a “complex operation” to access the MV Barima wreck had begun, led by the Guyana Defence Force Coast Guard with specialist teams from France and Trinidad and Tobago. Ali said divers had assessed the wreck on 21 July and that 1,500-ton buoyancy airbags would be used to reposition it, that troops were searching Shell Beach, and that a prayer service would be held at Charity that evening.
Headline states the MV Barima death toll rose to 57 with 19 vessels and two aircraft deployed; the capture is incomplete, containing no article body.

The Chronicle reports Prime Minister Mark Phillips announced on the afternoon of Wednesday 22 July that three further bodies had been recovered, bringing the total recovered since the 18 July sinking to 65, five of them that day. Phillips said 44 victims had been positively identified by their families and 23 bodies released to relatives for burial, and that the number of people rescued remained at 76. The article says search and recovery operations continue.

The state-owned Chronicle reports Prime Minister Mark Phillips rejected claims that private citizens or political figures, including Opposition Leader Azruddin Mohamed, were “ahead” of the government’s search operation, and criticised what he called exploitation of the tragedy “for clicks, likes, and political attention” and the circulation of graphic images. The article states that as of Tuesday 21 July authorities had recovered 53 bodies and rescued 76 people, and says investigators have pointed to an inaccurate manifest and suspected crew drug use as possible contributing factors.

The Chronicle reports Prime Minister Mark Phillips said at a Tuesday evening 21 July briefing that nobody was forced to sign any compensation document, and that government provided funds, clothing, food and transport to survivors who came ashore with nothing. He said relatives were being transported from Port Kaituma, Mabaruma and Georgetown to Suddie Hospital, where Health Minister Frank Anthony oversees identification, and reminded responders that everyone recovered must be handed to police at the Charity recovery site.

The state-owned Chronicle reports President Ali remained at the Charity waterfront with families, and that the search area was expanded by 400 square miles as far as Waini Point, with 16 vessels deployed. It cites the Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre as confirming 76 rescued and 53 bodies recovered as of Tuesday 21 July. It says officials disclosed the captain and another crew member tested positive for cannabis and were arrested, and that CCTV review put 179 people aboard against a manifest listing 116 passengers and 17 crew.

The Chronicle reports President Ali issued a proclamation on Tuesday 21 July declaring Wednesday 22 to Friday 24 July days of national mourning for victims of the MV Barima, which it says capsized on 18 July carrying approximately 179 people en route from Georgetown to Port Kaituma. Flags are to fly at half-staff; 22 July was also declared a National Day of Prayer, with a service at the Kingston Seawall and nights of reflection to follow in Port Kaituma and Mabaruma.

The Chronicle reports pilot Learie Barclay appealed on social media for the public to stop flying drones in the MV Barima search area, saying low-flying aircraft including his own were being endangered. It notes Opposition MP Sherod Duncan was detained on Tuesday 21 July over alleged unauthorised drone use and later released, with Home Affairs Minister Oneidge Walrond saying he did not have the required licence. The article also restates government statements on the crew cannabis tests and the manifest discrepancy.

The Chronicle reports the Central Islamic Organisation of Guyana issued a statement extending condolences to the families of those who died in the MV Barima tragedy, and offering prayers for survivors, for families still awaiting news of missing relatives, and for personnel involved in search and recovery. Quoting Surah Al-Baqarah 2:156, the organisation called on Guyanese to set aside differences, saying such tragedies remind people that they are “one people, strengthened by our shared humanity.”

The Chronicle reports Prime Minister Mark Phillips said on Gordon Moseley’s radio programme on Wednesday 22 July that the government is moving to establish an independent Commission of Inquiry into the MV Barima tragedy, declining to give a timeline but calling it a priority. He said people would be held responsible based on the inquiry’s outcome, and listed assistance including flights for relatives, additional refrigerated storage, funeral aid, temporary accommodation and counselling. The item is credited to DPI.

The Chronicle carries, under a 23 July date and a second URL, the same account of President Ali’s Wednesday morning briefing at the Charity Waterfront announcing a “complex operation” to enter the MV Barima wreck, led by the GDF Coast Guard with French and Trinidadian specialist teams. Ali is quoted saying divers assessed the wreck on Tuesday, that 1,500-ton buoyancy airbags would be secured to reposition it, that troops were searching Shell Beach, and that a Charity prayer service would follow that evening.

The Chronicle reports Human Services and Social Security Minister Vindhya Persaud said her ministry mobilised social workers, counsellors and psychologists and established a command centre at the Umana Yana, Kingston, on Sunday 19 July. Speaking on the New Day radio programme, she said social workers accompany families travelling to Region Two, teams are deployed in Regions One and Two and at Smith Creek, and support is being prepared for first responders and Transport and Harbours Department staff, with a public hotline under discussion.

The Chronicle reports the Ethnic Relations Commission, led by Chairman Shaikh Moeenul Hack, deployed Commissioners and staff to Region Two, visiting the Charity River Dam, Suddie Hospital and the Suddie Funeral Parlour to offer comfort, emotional support and counselling to bereaved families. It names five Commissioners in the delegation, says the team met President Ali and was briefed by Health Minister Frank Anthony, and quotes Hack saying the Commission stands in solidarity with every affected family.

The Chronicle reports First Lady Arya Ali issued a message of condolence to families affected by the MV Barima sinking, saying the tragedy had left Guyanese “standing on the shore of grief.” She addressed mothers who had lost children, saying “I see you. I feel your pain. I share your anxiety,” gave thanks for those rescued while remembering those who did not survive, and called on Guyanese to comfort one another and to pray for rescuers and waiting families.

The Chronicle reports Prime Minister Mark Phillips said in a radio interview on Wednesday 22 July that those responsible will be held accountable once an independent Commission of Inquiry completes its work, and that the inquiry will examine pre-departure events, adherence to operating procedures, passenger manifest discrepancies, cargo handling, emergency response and any regulatory breaches. He cautioned against drawing conclusions before investigators finish, and said placing some maritime staff on administrative leave was standard practice, not a finding of guilt. Credited to DPI.

The Chronicle reports on an Interfaith National Prayer Service hosted by the Government of Guyana, bringing together representatives of various faiths and members of the public. Delivering the feature address, Prime Minister Mark Phillips spoke of “unfathomable sorrow” and offered condolences on behalf of himself, President Ali and the government. He commended the disciplined services, medical personnel, divers, fishermen, volunteers and private companies, and thanked international partners including the French Guiana specialist team, the French Armed Forces, Brazil and Trinidad and Tobago.

The Chronicle reports President Ali said work to reposition the MV Barima wreck continued overnight, and that Prime Minister Mark Phillips confirmed two additional bodies recovered during Thursday 23 July, bringing the total recovered to 72, of whom 65 had been positively identified. Phillips said 22 assets — 19 vessels and three aircraft — remained deployed across a search area of about 2,100 square kilometres extending to Waini Point, and repeated that unauthorised drones are prohibited. The article states 179 were aboard and 76 rescued.

The Chronicle reports the Tourism and Hospitality Association of Guyana, through its President Mitra Ramkumar, issued a statement on Wednesday 22 July extending condolences to the families, loved ones and communities affected by the sinking of the MV Barima. The association thanked local fisherfolk who helped rescue survivors, along with government agencies, emergency responders, members of the disciplined services, divers, medical personnel, volunteers and international partners, and said it stood in solidarity with families awaiting news.

The Chronicle reports President Ali addressed the National Toshaos Council Conference by phone from Charity on Thursday night 23 July, apologising for his absence and saying the government’s immediate national priority is supporting affected families and the search and recovery operation. He said teams were still working to move the vessel into shallower water because divers reported people remaining inside, and assured Indigenous leaders that conference commitments on jobs, public services, housing and the Low Carbon Development Strategy would be pursued.

The Chronicle reports the Ethnic Relations Commission held a service of prayer and reflection at its Queenstown, Georgetown office on Thursday 23 July, themed “In Our Hearts. In Our Prayers. Forever Remembered.” Commissioner Ashton Simon gave opening remarks, with prayers and reflections from Islamic, Christian and Hindu representatives including Chairman Shaikh Moeenul Hack, Reverend Rodwell Porter and Pandit Krishn Sharma. Indra Chandarpal and Colleen Clarke-Anthony also spoke, the latter calling for psychosocial support for affected children.

The Chronicle reports President Ali told relatives at a briefing on the evening of Thursday 23 July that a full salvage of the MV Barima may become the only remaining option if efforts to access the wreck fail, but said authorities were trying to avoid it because it could disturb what remains inside. He said some divers became ill and returned to the surface during that day’s repositioning attempt, and that divers would return from 5:30 a.m. The article gives 76 rescued, 72 bodies recovered and 65 identified.

The Chronicle reports Human Services and Social Security Minister Vindhya Persaud told the National Toshaos Council Conference at the Arthur Chung Conference Centre on Thursday 23 July that the government is developing a long-term support strategy for survivors and affected families. She said her ministry is working with the Ministry of Education on grief and trauma counselling in schools, building on a University of Guyana programme developed after the Mahdia tragedy, and that assistance is being sought from the International Red Cross. Credited to DPI.

The Chronicle reports Prime Minister Mark Phillips said in an update on the evening of Thursday 23 July that two additional bodies were recovered, bringing confirmed fatalities to 72, of whom 65 had been positively identified, while technical teams continue repositioning the vessel. He said 22 assets — 19 vessels and three aircraft — remain deployed across a search zone of roughly 2,100 square kilometres extending to Waini Point, warned against unauthorised drones, and said ministers attended funerals in Regions One, Three and Six.

The Chronicle reports President Ali told relatives at Charity, Region Two on Wednesday evening 22 July that government support would continue after search and recovery efforts end, saying “We are not going to stop… we will be here with you.” He said strong currents had prevented divers from making the progress anticipated, commended Health Minister Frank Anthony and Regional Health Officer Ranjeev Singh, and described arrangements for transporting bodies and relatives, funeral support through regional administrations, and counselling services.

The Chronicle reports President Ali told relatives at the Operations Centre in Charity, Region Two on Friday 24 July that specialist dive teams recovered the body of one male during morning operations, bringing the number of bodies recovered to 73. He said divers began at 5 a.m., completed two dives of 45 to 60 minutes each and were beginning a third, cutting through sections of the wreck. The article states 179 were aboard, 76 rescued and 65 victims identified.

The Chronicle reports the Guyana Police Force said it continues to deploy personnel and resources to the MV Barima search and recovery operation, with ranks from the Marine Section, Tactical Services Unit, Criminal Investigation Department and Regional Divisions One and Two searching by boat several miles offshore and around the site of the sinking. It says drones are being used to help locate survivors, missing persons and bodies, alongside the GDF Coast Guard and Air Corps, the French Armed Forces, the Brazilian Navy and the Trinidad and Tobago Coast Guard.

An opinion column in the state-owned Chronicle, carrying a disclaimer that the views are the author’s own and giving the writer’s contact details as those of Freddie Kissoon, argues that a Commission of Inquiry into the MV Barima tragedy will become a farce. The column rejects a Guyana Human Rights Association proposal that six commissioners come from the opposition, and PNC parliamentary leader Terrence Campbell’s proposal that the National Assembly determine the commission’s composition, arguing commissioners should be technical experts.

The Chronicle reports Agriculture Minister Zulfikar Mustapha met village leaders on the sidelines of the National Toshaos Council Conference on Thursday 23 July to discuss village profiles and programmes covering coconuts, livestock, aquaculture, honey and onions. He said a koker at Morawhanna is being designed at an estimated engineering cost of about $80 million, and that a pontoon with two excavators will go permanently to Region One, starting at Red Hill, where a toshao said villagers have used the creek as a shortcut since the MV Barima tragedy.

The Chronicle reports Amerindian Affairs Minister Sarah Browne-Shadeek told the closing ceremony of the National Toshaos Conference on Friday 24 July that the MV Barima tragedy had left her “overwhelmed by darkness and sorrow.” She said the disaster was personal to her as a daughter of Region One, described travelling to Port Kaituma the morning after the news broke, and said the country must await the investigations to determine what went wrong and who was responsible. The article describes it as the deadliest maritime disaster in modern Guyanese history.

The Chronicle reports Prime Minister Mark Phillips said on HJ 94.1 Boom FM’s Jump Start programme on Friday morning 24 July that “our people are hurting, and they deserve the truth,” and that the government will act on the Commission of Inquiry’s recommendations. He said the MV Barima was dry-docked in 2024, repaired and deemed seaworthy, with its next dry-docking due in the latter half of 2026, that three new vessels have been acquired since 2020, and that reforms would cover drug testing, port clearance, supervision and CCTV coverage.

Headline and opening lines state that Guyanese, including senior government officials and dignitaries, joined families paying final respects as MV Barima victims were laid to rest; the capture is incomplete.

The Chronicle reports that mandirs affiliated with the Guyana Hindu Dharmic Sabha held prayer services for victims of the MV Barima tragedy, including at the Anna Regina Mandir on the Essequibo Coast and, on Thursday evening 23 July, at the Spring Garden Bhuvaneshwar Mandir with the Altruists Youth Group, where the Hanuman Chalisa was chanted. It says Dharmic Sabha President Vindhya Persaud attended the Shri Krishna Mandir and said the country is with the bereaved families.

An unsigned first-person opinion piece in the state-owned Chronicle states that its author is confident investigations will establish what caused the ferry to sink. The author asks whether the sinking was a natural disaster or “an act of terrorism,” accuses the opposition of turning the tragedy into a political field day, draws comparisons with the Adriana Younge case and other incidents, and likens an unnamed figure involved in the response to Jim Jones. No author is named in the capture.

The Chronicle reports President Ali said in an address to the nation on Saturday 25 July that he would announce on Sunday 26 July the names of a five-member international and independent Commission of Inquiry into the MV Barima tragedy, drawn from law, marine engineering, maritime safety and disaster investigation. He set out terms covering loading, boarding, seaworthiness, maintenance, crew conduct and the response. It reports 73 bodies recovered and 69 identified as of Saturday 25 July, 63 released to families, and 76 rescued.

The Chronicle reports Prime Minister Mark Phillips told a press conference that five dives of 45 to 60 minutes each were completed on Friday 24 July, one of which recovered an additional body, bringing the death toll to 73, of whom 69 were identified and 63 released, with 22 funerals completed. He said the search area was expanded by a further 32 square miles, 17 assets remain deployed, divers face strong currents and poor visibility, and preparations are advancing for a possible righting operation.

An unsigned first-person opinion piece in the state-owned Chronicle offers condolences to bereaved families and argues that conclusions about the MV Barima sinking should await investigation. Its author disputes that a vessel’s age determines seaworthiness, citing hundreds of millions spent between 2021 and 2024 and over $100 million budgeted for rehabilitation this year, rejects opposition calls for Ministers Edghill and Indar to resign, and disputes opposition claims about the MV Ma Lisha. No author is named in the capture.

The Chronicle reports President Ali announced on Sunday 26 July the five members of the international Commission of Inquiry: Justice Godfrey Phillip Smith of Belize as chair, Captain Hamada Fouda of Jamaica, Nyree Dawn Alfonso of Trinidad and Tobago, Dr Andrzej Jasionowski of Poland, and Rear Admiral (Ret’d) Hayden Pritchard of Trinidad and Tobago. It sets out the terms of reference, says the vessel sailed on 18 July with 116 passengers, 17 crew and cargo, and gives 73 bodies recovered and 69 identified as of Sunday 26 July.

A second Chronicle item, headlined “MV Barima incident….” and filed under a URL announcing that the President will name the COI members, repeats the report of President Ali’s Saturday 25 July address setting out the five-member commission and its terms of reference. This version states that 179 passengers and 17 crew were aboard, and gives 73 bodies recovered and 69 identified as of Saturday 25 July, with 63 released to families and 76 rescued.

The Chronicle reports that Andrea Narine of You and Eye Vision hosted a candlelight vigil in Queens, New York on Friday evening 24 July to honour those who died in the MV Barima disaster. It says members of the Guyanese diaspora gathered with candles, observed moments of silence and offered prayers, and quotes Narine saying the vigil was organised so the victims would not be forgotten and so bereaved families would know they are not alone.

The Chronicle reports the Shipping Association of Guyana welcomed President Ali’s decision to establish an independent Commission of Inquiry, calling the investigation “an important step toward establishing the facts,” providing answers to families and strengthening maritime safety. The association commended the Guyana Defence Force, Guyana Police Force, MARAD, the Civil Defence Commission, volunteers and private operators. The article states the vessel sailed on 18 July with 116 passengers, 17 crew and cargo, and gives 73 bodies recovered and 69 identified as of Sunday 26 July.
